title: Git Doesn't Store Diffs: The Database Inside Your Repo

segments.narration: Every commit you have ever made is a full snapshot of your project, not a diff. Git is a content-addressed database, and that one choice explains how it works.

Inside the hidden dot git folder, Git stores four kinds of objects. A blob holds the raw bytes of one file. A tree lists file names and points at blobs and other trees. A commit points at one tree, its parent commits, an author and a message. An annotated tag points at a commit. Every object is named by a hash of its type, its size and its contents.

By default that name is a SHA-1 hash, forty hex characters. Git hashes a short header, the object type and the byte count, followed by the bytes themselves. Change one byte and the name changes completely. That is why an unchanged file costs nothing in a new commit. Same bytes, same hash, one stored blob, shared by every snapshot that contains it.

visual_payload.code_snippet:
$ echo hello | git hash-object --stdin
ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a
$ printf 'blob 6\0hello\n' | sha1sum
ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a  -

segments.narration: Branches are not containers. A branch is a ref, a tiny record holding one commit hash. HEAD usually points at a branch, so committing writes a new commit object and moves that one pointer forward. That is why creating a branch is instant. Deleting a branch does not delete its commits right away either. They linger until garbage collection prunes whatever nothing references.

Whole snapshots sound expensive, so here is the catch. Loose objects are compressed one at a time. During garbage collection, and in every push or fetch, Git packs objects into packfiles and stores similar objects as deltas against each other. So diffs do exist, but only as a storage trick underneath. The model you reason about is still whole snapshots.

Here is the proof in a real repository. Ask Git for the type of HEAD and it answers commit. Ask that commit for its tree and its parent, and you get two more hashes. List the tree and you get file modes, object types, hashes and names. Each hash is the address of the object one level down.

visual_payload.code_snippet:
$ git cat-file -t HEAD
commit
$ git log -1 --format='tree %t%nparent %p'
tree 2532dc0
parent b80d9ca
$ git ls-tree --abbrev=8 HEAD
100644 blob ce013625	hello.txt
100644 blob 8ff82333	notes.md

segments.narration: Now the deduplication. The second commit only changed the notes file. Ask both commits for hello dot t x t, and both trees point at the identical blob hash. One stored object, referenced by two snapshots. Nothing was copied.

visual_payload.code_snippet:
$ git ls-tree --abbrev=8 HEAD~1 hello.txt
100644 blob ce013625	hello.txt
$ git ls-tree --abbrev=8 HEAD hello.txt
100644 blob ce013625	hello.txt

segments.narration: So stop picturing Git as a stack of patches. It is a database of immutable snapshots, deduplicated by hash, with deltas hidden in the packfiles. Once you see objects and refs, branching, resetting and recovering a lost commit stop being magic. They are pointer moves over a graph that never changes in place. When a rebase goes wrong, open the reflog before you panic. The old commits are still there.
